evals.prompt: I run DevRel at Halyard Systems - we sell a Kubernetes cost-optimisation controller, self-serve from EUR 49/month plus an enterprise tier. I've just been handed EUR 90,000 for developer events in 2027 and my boss wants awareness in the Rust community, more signups, and two senior SRE hires out of it. I have three engineers who can travel, maybe 12 days each across the whole year, and I'm the only person who touches event measurement. What's already on my desk: Ferrous Summit (the big US Rust conference), three regional Rust days in Europe, two student hackathons, and a Berlin meetup we've sponsored twice. This is meant to build something that lasts, not a one-off. What should I do with the money?
evals.expected_output: Two or three candidate year portfolios with allocation splits, staffing cost and what each deliberately fails at; one recommended with the losers explained; a single primary objective; the farm-team shape deleted because one person owns measurement; an unallocated reserve held back.
expectations: Names exactly one primary objective for the plan, or one per event, and states that a sponsorship cannot carry two primary objectives
Presents two or three candidate portfolios for the year rather than a single recommended list of events
Gives each candidate portfolio its own allocation split, the staffing it consumes, and what it deliberately fails at
Recommends one portfolio and states why each rejected portfolio loses
Asks for explicit agreement on the chosen portfolio before discussing any negotiation or purchase
Deletes the farm-team shape (student hackathons plus one practitioner conference) rather than ranking it last, because one person owns event measurement
Names ecosystem-anchored as the default portfolio shape, and either applies it or names the specific condition that would move the plan to flagship-led
States the efficiency ordering of the portfolio shapes explicitly, with ecosystem-anchored ahead of flagship-led, farm-team and regional spread
States that flagship-led and ecosystem-anchored tie on effort, and justifies why they are equal on effort while differing on efficiency
Holds 15-25% of the EUR 90,000 unallocated as a reserve and names what the reserve is for
Expresses effort as staff-days, travel overhead, reusable preparation and follow-up capacity, never as a currency amount
States which interview answer moved which option, naming the three-engineer, 12-day-each staffing ceiling as a driver

evals.prompt: Two quotes landed this week and my CMO has already made up his mind. We're Lumenpath - API observability, $200/month entry plan, self-serve plus a small enterprise team. Plumbline Conf is a volunteer-run community conference, 700 attendees, quoting us Gold at $6,000: a table if space allows, four passes, and logo on talk videos is another $1,000 on top. Continuum Summit is a big vendor conference quoting Gold at $25,000: a 10x10 booth, six passes, logo on the hall wall, badge scanning included. My CMO says Continuum's Gold is obviously four times the value for four times the price. Plumbline also lists a 90-minute hands-on workshop add-on at $12,000, which looks insane to me. Which Gold do we buy?
evals.expected_output: A refusal of the tier-name comparison, a line-item rebuild of both packages, the three prospectus clauses read before price, the lower-tier-plus-add-on play surfaced, passes treated as money, and a fully loaded cost plus a pre-set threshold before any verdict.
expectations: Rejects comparing the two events by tier name and states that tier names carry no meaning across events
Rebuilds the comparison from package line items rather than from the Gold label or the $6,000 versus $25,000 ratio
Explicitly refuses the CMO's 'four times the value' reading
Reads three clauses before price: what contact data the sponsor receives, how a stage slot is obtained, and which surfaces are sold separately

States the within-event efficiency ordering as lower tier plus the one add-on that reaches the audience, ahead of the cheapest tier clearing the booth price floor, ahead of logo-only, ahead of top tier
Treats the $12,000 workshop add-on as correctly priced hands-on attention rather than as an overpriced upsell, noting it outprices whole tiers
Treats included passes as a subtractable money line and conditions their value on being able to staff them
Checks whether an eligibility-gated startup or end-user tier exists before settling on a rung
States that a community or volunteer-run conference typically sells no attendee contact data at any price, and does not assume badge scanning exists at Plumbline
Notes that a booth sits behind a price floor, so deciding whether a booth is needed sets the minimum spend before the tier list is read
Costs both options fully loaded - fee, add-ons, booth build and shipping, swag, travel and accommodation, and loaded staff time - before any verdict
Names staff time as the cost line most often omitted and the one that most often doubles the total

Sets a target cost per qualified conversation and a minimum conversation count before recommending either purchase, and derives the target from the company's blended acquisition cost rather than from the sponsorship fee

evals.prompt: DevTide Expo is pitching us hard and I need an answer today. 12,000 attendees expected, brand-new event in Austin, first edition. Booth is $34,000. Their rep keeps repeating that it's the cheapest cost-per-attendee on our whole list - $2.83 a head versus $40-plus at the smaller conferences. They've also offered to send us the full attendee list as a CSV after the show, which nobody else does. They need a signed contract within nine days or the price goes up 20%. They can't share role breakdowns yet because registration only opened last month. We're Orrery Labs, we sell a CI caching layer to platform engineering teams. Do we sign?
evals.expected_output: A decline, with cost-per-attendee rejected as the deciding figure, the attendee-list offer named as both a walk-away signal and an ethics failure, the deadline-before-data pattern named, the evidence request listed, and the decision recorded with its reason.
expectations: Rejects cost-per-attendee as the deciding figure and states that headcount is the least informative number in a prospectus
Recommends declining or walking away rather than negotiating the price down
Names the offered attendee-list CSV as a walk-away signal rather than a differentiating benefit
Refuses the attendee list as an ethics failure where the attendees never consented, not as a point to caveat or negotiate
Names deadline pressure arriving before the audience data as its own walk-away trigger
Names unverifiable demographics and a first-time organizer making large promises as walk-away triggers

Lists the audience evidence to demand before pricing anything, covering role mix and seniority, company size or buying influence, geography and travel mix, prior editions and returning-sponsor rate, package line items, program balance between technical and sponsor content, and follow-up rights
States that a missing post-event report or missing demographic actuals is itself the answer rather than a neutral gap
Scores the event against the company's own objective rather than against other events' prices
Notes that a zero on ICP overlap ends the evaluation regardless of any total score
Records the decline with its reason so the event is not rebought next year on the strength of its headcount
Offers the organizer evidence request as the concrete next step before any signature
Ends in a decision - a decline, or a stated threshold under which it would be signed - never a maybe

evals.prompt: We've already paid EUR 14,000 to sponsor Nordhack, a 48-hour student hackathon in Tallinn in three weeks, 400 students. The package gives us a mentor table, a prize track we name ourselves, and a 30-minute slot on Friday evening. I'm at Tessellate - we sell a real-time geospatial API. Marketing wants the prize to be 'Best Use of the Tessellate API' with EUR 3,000 cash, and they want to hire a booth crew from a local agency because our engineers are heads-down on a release. We'd also love to turn that Friday slot into a proper hands-on workshop, though we've never written one. Three engineers could come if I push. What's the plan for the two days?
evals.expected_output: The prize category reframed around the problem, judging criteria published before entries open and judging kept unbuyable, the agency crew rejected for technical staff, the workshop deleted for lack of curriculum, hackathon crunch-hour staffing, and a qualification bar set before the event.
expectations: Reframes the prize category around the problem rather than the product, and rejects 'Best Use of the Tessellate API' as the category name
States that judging criteria must be published before entries open and cannot be changed afterwards
Refuses to let the sponsorship influence the judging outcome, including favouring teams the mentor table helped
Rejects the agency booth crew and requires technical staff who can debug a stranger's code
Brainstorms two or three activation options for the package already bought, names the trade-off in each, and recommends one before anything is purchased
Deletes or defers the hands-on workshop because no curriculum exists and building one runs to roughly a month or two of preparation rather than three weeks
Names the compliance exposure specific to a prize track: prize promotions are regulated in some jurisdictions, criteria fix once entries open, and prize value can be reportable

Staffs the hackathon crunch hours - kickoff and team formation, the evening build peak, the hours before submission, and demos - and runs a skeleton crew overnight, at meal times and through the mid-event lull
Rotates staff off the floor rather than running the same people continuously
Defines the qualified-conversation bar and the named next step before the event and briefs every staffer on both
Lists prizes the audience actually wants - cash, quality hardware, conference tickets, credits with no redemption maze, time with someone interesting - rather than product credits alone
Sets follow-up inside 48 hours, personal and on the substance of each conversation, with no generic sequence and no automatic addition to a sales sequence
Sets a fully loaded cost and a threshold even though the fee is already spent, so the sponsorship can be judged at renewal

evals.prompt: My boss wants a verdict on last year's PlatformSummit sponsorship by Friday. Here's everything we have: 1,412 badge scans, 3,000 stickers gone, two blog mentions, and the team says the buzz on the floor was great. Fee was $22,000 and we sent four people for three days. Sales imported all 1,412 scans into the CRM and worked approximately none of them. We never captured a baseline of anything. We're Brackwater - infrastructure-as-code linting, sold to platform teams. Renew or not?
evals.expected_output: A plain statement that the question cannot be answered honestly without a pre-set threshold and baseline, a refusal to manufacture a return from badge scans, the qualified conversation defined, the routing table applied instead of defaulting to sales, and the process fixed for the next event.
expectations: States plainly that the question cannot be answered honestly, because no threshold and no baseline were set before signing
Refuses to manufacture a return figure or an attribution claim from the 1,412 badge scans
Rejects badge scans as a measure of value and names the qualified conversation as the only unit that compares across a hackathon, a community day and a mega-conference
Defines the qualified conversation as all three of: has the problem the product solves, holds or influences the decision, and agreed to a named next step
Names importing all 1,412 scans into the CRM and routing them to sales as the failure that fills a CRM with records nobody works

Gives the conversation routing table - case-study material to marketing, feedback and beta candidates to product, bugs to engineering, partner interest to partnerships, candidates to recruiting, buyers to sales - rather than defaulting everything to sales
Recomputes the fully loaded cost including loaded staff time for four people across preparation, travel, on-site days and follow-up, not just the $22,000 fee
Does not substitute a secondary metric that happens to look better for the missing primary one
Returns one of the three verdicts - renew, renegotiate or drop - rather than a maybe, and states what evidence each would need
Fixes the process for the next sponsorship: a target cost per qualified conversation and a minimum conversation count set before signing
Requires a pre-event baseline of the primary metric captured one to four weeks before the next event

Requires one event-specific URL and one promo or credit code per event, never reused across events, and requires the post-event review to run within two weeks while the conversation log is still accurate

evals.prompt: We're sponsoring Meridian Python Days - volunteer-run, 1,100 attendees - and we bought the EUR 9,000 tier: a table, six passes, and a two-minute pitch from the stage between talks. I want to do all of it: staff the table, run a 90-minute workshop, host an evening dinner for 20 people, and put money into their diversity scholarship fund. Only two of us are going, me and one engineer. We're Ferrite, a Postgres change-data-capture tool, self-serve at $99/month. Two questions on top: how do we get the badge scan data off the table, and how do we get one of our engineers onto the main stage? We'd happily go up a tier if they'd hand us a slot.
evals.expected_output: The workshop and dinner deleted because two people can staff exactly one thing, the help-desk booth recommended, badge scan data explained as non-existent at a community event with opt-in capture instead, the paid stage slot refused as an ethics failure and routed to the CFP, and the scholarship fund kept off the value ladder.
expectations: Deletes both the workshop and the evening side event, on the grounds that a team of two travelling can staff exactly one activation
Recommends the help-desk booth as the activation: technical staff who debug a stranger's code, a demo the attendee drives, and a win reachable in about five minutes
Brainstorms two or three activation options with the trade-off in each, recommends one, and validates it before anything is bought
States the activation efficiency ordering explicitly - help-desk booth ahead of prize track, ahead of side event, ahead of workshop
States that value on this axis is qualified developer conversations that continue after the event, never badge scans
States that a volunteer-run community conference holds no attendee contact data and offers no badge scanning, so the scan-data request has no answer there
Requires opt-in consent capture instead - an opt-in draw, a workshop signup, or a QR to the event landing page - and states that a smaller clean list beats a larger invented one
Refuses to buy a main-stage slot at an event that runs a CFP, and names it as an ethics failure rather than a negotiating position
Routes the stage ambition to the CFP process, referencing samber/developer-relations-skills@conference-cfp-submission
Keeps the scholarship fund off the activation ranking, states it produces no conversations by design, and frames it as a deliberate awareness or employer-brand purchase
Warns that trade-show behaviour at a community event costs more credibility than the logo buys
Notes the sponsor code of conduct a community conference asks a sponsor to sign
Treats the two-minute stage pitch as a brief timed pitch included in the package, not as a talk slot or a substitute for one

evals.prompt: Draft me the negotiation email. We're Solstice Metrics - time-series database, enterprise-sold, around $40k average contract value. The event is Northlight Cloud Days, first edition, 700 attendees projected, and we're looking at their EUR 18,000 tier. My asks, in the order I care about them: knock 20% off the price, get us the attendee list, get our CTO 15 minutes on the main stage, and get our logo onto the keynote backdrop. They also run three other events in the same series next year, so I'll push for a 25% bundle discount across all four. What should the email say?
evals.expected_output: The attendee list, the bought stage slot and the keynote backdrop refused as ethics failures; the remaining asks sequenced by efficiency with the previous post-event report first, overridden here by the attendance remedy because this is a first edition; published multi-event discounts checked before inventing a bundle ask; a draft email produced.
expectations: Refuses the attendee-list ask outright as an ethics failure, not as a low-probability ask, and states these refusals are not gray areas to probe in negotiation
Refuses to buy the CTO a main-stage slot at an event running a CFP, and refuses the keynote backdrop as buying a keynote's content or an implied speaking slot
States that the asks compete for a finite budget - the number of things the organizer says yes to before the conversation turns - rather than for money

Gives the efficiency ordering of asks with the previous edition's post-event report first, ahead of extra staff passes, lead-data delivery timing, placement on a specific high-traffic surface, a workshop or demo-theatre slot, permission to publish content, and a written attendance estimate with a remedy
Justifies the post-event report leading: it costs nothing to ask, arrives before signature, and can still cancel the deal
Overrides the default order for this case and makes the written attendance estimate with a remedy the first ask, because this is a first edition
Names what the default ordering starves - the attendance remedy and the workshop slot - rather than silently dropping them
States that the ordering sequences the asks and never shortens the list
Checks whether the event series already publishes multi-event discounts before inventing the 25% bundle ask
Notes that some event families fix multi-event discounts at published single-digit percentages rather than negotiating them

Names the conditions under which packages genuinely move: early commitment, multi-event or multi-year deals, off-peak editions, growing events, and bringing something the organizer wants such as a workshop, a mentor pool or a scholarship fund
Does not lead the email with the 20% price cut as the primary ask
Produces an actual draft email carrying the surviving asks in the recommended order

evals.prompt: We're Kilnworks and we run two motions. One is a free-plus-$29/month self-serve CLI that developers buy on a card with no sales contact at all. The other is an enterprise platform sold by a four-person sales team with a nine-month cycle. For 2027 we've committed to two sponsorships: a 500-person student hackathon in Porto and an enterprise-heavy platform engineering conference in Chicago. Leadership wants one KPI across both so the board slide stays clean - they've picked 'pipeline sourced from events'. Give me the measurement plan.
evals.expected_output: A refusal of the single shared KPI, objectives set per event rather than per year, the hackathon assigned awareness or recruiting rather than pipeline, sourced-revenue claims rejected in favour of influence, in-product measurement for the self-serve motion, and per-event URLs, baselines and 30/60/90 windows.
expectations: Refuses the single 'pipeline sourced from events' KPI applied across both events
Sets the objective per event rather than per year, and says explicitly which event carries which objective
Assigns the student hackathon an awareness or recruiting objective rather than pipeline, and the Chicago conference a pipeline objective
States that for the enterprise product the attendee is usually a champion rather than a signer, so the event's contribution is influence rather than source
Rejects sourced-revenue claims the CRM cannot support and keeps pipeline claims riding on the CRM
For the self-serve CLI, measures in-product - event-specific signup URL, promo or credit code, activation curve - rather than through a sales sequence
Makes the self-serve follow-up a product invitation rather than a sales sequence
Names what must not be claimed per objective, including attributed revenue for an awareness objective and activations from anyone who merely saw the logo for an adoption objective
Requires one event-specific URL and one promo or credit code per event, never reused across events
Requires a pre-event baseline of each event's primary metric captured one to four weeks before that event
Measures the event cohort at 30, 60 and 90 days, plus one pipeline check a full sales cycle out
Defines the event cohort as everyone arriving through the event's own URL, code, workshop signup or consented scan, tagged once and never merged into a generic campaign

evals.prompt: I have to put something concrete in front of the board on 14 March, about eight weeks out, or the event budget gets reassigned. We're Marlstone, a feature-flag service, self-serve from $59/month. There's $45,000 left in the event budget. My CEO's idea is a splashy hands-on workshop track at a big conference in October as the centrepiece, and he keeps bringing it up. Two engineers are available. We're already contracted at a mid-size platform conference in February where we bought their smallest tier, and there's a new regional DevOps day in May we haven't committed to yet. What do I do?
evals.expected_output: The October workshop deleted outright against the eight-week result date, the already-contracted February event's add-ons promoted over the new May commitment, the near-date rungs and help-desk booth promoted, the result date separated from the contract deadline, and a threshold set before any spend.
expectations: Deletes the October workshop outright, on the grounds that a month or two of preparation does not fit inside a result date eight weeks away
Refuses the CEO's workshop centrepiece for the March board date rather than accommodating it as a reduced version
Promotes buying an add-on at the already-contracted February conference over committing to the new May event
Promotes the meetup and community rungs, and the help-desk booth activation, specifically because of the near result date
States which interview answer moved which option, naming the 14 March date as the driver
Separates the date the result must be visible from the contract deadline, and asks for both
Checks which branded surfaces or add-ons are still available at the February event, noting that the best ones sell out months ahead
Caps the recommendation at what two engineers can actually staff for the full hall hours
Notes that an October event can still be right under a compounding mandate, and says what would have to be true to buy it on a separate decision
Sets a target cost per qualified conversation and a minimum conversation count for whatever is bought, before the money moves
Keeps a share of the remaining $45,000 unallocated rather than spending all of it

evals.prompt: Quick maths check before I sign. Sponsorship fee $16,000, workshop add-on $9,000, flights and hotels for four people $7,200, swag and print $2,400 - so $34,600 all in. Last year we closed 260 new customers at a blended acquisition cost of about $1,100, and roughly 35% of our sales conversations turn into an opportunity. The expo hall is open 9 to 6 for three days. Tell me our cost per lead and whether this is a good deal. We're Verdigris Compute - GPU scheduling, sold to ML platform teams.
evals.expected_output: Cost per lead reframed as cost per qualified conversation with its three-part bar, the $34,600 rejected as incomplete once loaded staff time and the missing lines are added, the target derived from the $1,100 and 35% figures rather than from the fee, a minimum conversation count set alongside it, and no verdict without audience evidence.
expectations: Reframes 'cost per lead' as cost per qualified conversation and defines the bar as all three of: has the problem, holds or influences the decision, and agreed to a named next step
Rejects the $34,600 total as incomplete
Adds loaded staff time for four people across preparation, travel, on-site days and follow-up, and shows how much it changes the total
States that staff time is the line most teams omit and the line that most often doubles the total
Adds the remaining missing cost lines to the worksheet, including booth build, shipping and storage between editions
Notes opportunity cost of the engineer-days even if it is not priced
Derives the target cost per qualified conversation from the $1,100 blended acquisition cost and the 35% conversation-to-opportunity rate, not from the sponsorship fee
Carries both the $1,100 and the 35% figures through the arithmetic explicitly
Sets a minimum conversation count alongside the target cost per conversation, not one without the other
Fixes both numbers before signing rather than computing them after the event
Declines to call it a good deal without the event's audience evidence, and names which evidence is missing
Notes that staffing the booth across three days of 9-to-6 hall hours is the binding constraint, and checks it against the four people available

evals.prompt: Three things landed on me at Ravenscar Tooling this week. First: we spend 55% of our DevRel budget on events, and finance found a report saying the industry average is around 41%, so they want me to cut to 41% by Q3. Second: we want to stop sponsoring other people's conferences and run our own one-day conference next year instead. Third: we want to put $30,000 a year into sponsoring the open-source projects our product depends on, and our VP says that comes out of the event budget too. Sort this out for me.
evals.expected_output: The ~41% figure refused as a target with its source, year and weaknesses named; the budget driven by objective, threshold and staffing instead; running their own conference, open-source project sponsorship and the pillar-level split each routed to the correct sibling skill.
expectations: Refuses to treat the roughly 41% published events share as a target to cut to
States what the figure is usable for - evidence that events historically dominate DevRel spend - and names its published source and year
Names the weaknesses of the figure explicitly: a small respondent count and reported shares summing to more than 100%
Bases the event budget on the objective, the per-event threshold and the staffing ceiling rather than on an industry percentage
Routes running their own conference to samber/developer-relations-skills@developer-meetup-program rather than answering it here
Routes the open-source project sponsorship to samber/developer-relations-skills@oss-sponsors-brand-strategy rather than answering it here
States that open-source project sponsorship is not part of the developer-event budget
Routes the pillar-level budget split to samber/developer-relations-skills@devrel-budget-allocation
Does not answer with a recommended percentage of DevRel budget for events
Keeps its own answer scoped to which events to sponsor, at what tier, with which activation and against what threshold
